methods.label: Complete the cube and subtract its corner
methods.explanation:
The three unit squares suggest completing a unit cube. First we must establish the triangular edge lengths, since the drawing is schematic.

Each isosceles right triangle shares a whole edge of length \(1\) with a square. By the Pythagorean theorem, its sides are therefore either \(1,1,\sqrt2\), or \(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2,1\). Call the latter kind small. In a closed polyhedron, every edge belongs to exactly two faces, so occurrences of each edge length among all the faces must come in pairs.

Triangle \(G\) cannot have side \(1/\sqrt2\): the small triangles would contribute an even number of edges of that length, while \(G\) would contribute three more. Since \(F\) shares different edges with \(D\) and \(G\), a small \(F\) would force precisely this impossible side length for \(G\). Thus \(F\) is not small.

There can now be at most two small triangles. One small triangle would have no other face to match its two short edges. Two small triangles would have to share both short edges with each other. That is impossible for distinct faces: sharing two sides of a triangle fixes all three vertices and would make the triangles coincide. Consequently, all three right triangles have unit legs and hypotenuse \(\sqrt2\).

The side of \(G\), which meets \(F\), is now either \(1\) or \(\sqrt2\). It cannot be \(1\), because then the three hypotenuse occurrences would have no way to pair. Hence \(G\) has side \(\sqrt2\). Its three edges must match the three available hypotenuses, one from each right triangle.

To recognize the solid, keep \(D\) as the bottom of a unit cube. Fold \(B\) up as its back and \(C\) up as its left side; their free vertical edges meet at the corner above their common corner with \(D\). Triangle \(F\) fills half the front, \(E\) fills half the right side, and \(A\) fills half the top. Their unit legs follow cube edges. Their hypotenuses are diagonals of these three cube faces, surrounding the corner opposite the common corner of the three squares. Triangle \(G\) closes that opening. Equivalently, cutting off this corner of a unit cube and unfolding along the displayed connections gives the stated faces and net.

Let \(X\) be the removed cube corner and \(P,Q,R\) its three neighboring cube vertices. The removed tetrahedron \(XPQR\) has three mutually perpendicular edges \(XP=XQ=XR=1\). Taking \(XPQ\) as its base gives base area \(\frac12\) and perpendicular height \(XR=1\). Thus
\[
V_{\text{removed}}=\frac13\cdot\frac12\cdot1=\frac16.
\]
The desired volume is therefore
\[
V=1^3-\frac16=\boxed{\frac56},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{D}\).

The written method also completes a composite solid and subtracts its tetrahedral component (cnm_h107), and counts face-edge incidences with multiplicity two (math:double-counting). Its local prerequisites include Pythagorean side lengths, equal sides of an equilateral triangle, odd-even pairing, cube structure, triangle area, and cube volume. These assignments describe the mathematics of the task and method, not student mastery.
limitations: The triangular faces are drawn schematically without explicit right-angle markers. Their apparent angles and pixel lengths are not metric evidence.
Edge matching uses the ordinary closed convex polyhedron convention: faces meet along whole edges, each edge belongs to two faces, and distinct triangular faces cannot coincide.

The removed tetrahedron has base area 1/2 and perpendicular height 1, so the remaining volume is 1−(1/3)(1/2)(1)=5/6.
